name: Fluid and salt
does: Raises blood volume, so less of it pools in your legs when you stand.
detail: Up to 2–3 litres of water and 10–12 g of salt a day "may be considered".
evidence: Class IIb, Level E — the consensus panel’s weakest grade: expert opinion, not trial evidence.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Compression — above the waist of your socks
does: Stops blood pooling in the abdomen, which is where most of it goes.
detail: On a tilt table, heart rate fell step by step with how much of the body was compressed: 109 bpm with none, 103 with the lower legs, 97 with the abdomen and thighs, 92 with both.
evidence: Randomised crossover trial, 30 patients. Small, but it is a real trial with a dose-response.

name: Exercise, starting lying down
does: Rebuilds blood volume and heart size, which standing all day does not.
detail: A structured, graduated programme beginning with non-upright exercise — rowing machines, recumbent bikes, swimming — before anything upright.
evidence: Class IIa, Level B-R — "can be effective", supported by randomised data.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Reviewing the drugs you already take
does: Several common medications make orthostatic symptoms worse.
detail: Withdrawing medications that aggravate POTS is listed first among the non-drug measures.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Ivabradine
does: Slows the heart without lowering blood pressure.
detail: Standing heart rate fell from 94.2 to 77.9 bpm against placebo, with improved physical and social functioning.
evidence: The one randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a drug in POTS. 22 patients, hyperadrenergic subtype.

name: Beta-blockers (low-dose propranolol)
detail: Covered by the consensus statement as an option; doses are low, and higher doses can make fatigue worse.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Midodrine
does: Tightens blood vessels so less blood pools.
detail: Short-acting, taken before being upright; not at bedtime.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Fludrocortisone
does: Helps the body hold on to salt and water.
detail: Used alongside the salt and fluid measures rather than instead of them.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement

name: Pyridostigmine
does: Acts on the autonomic signalling itself.
detail: Sometimes chosen when the gut symptoms are prominent.
source: 2015 Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement
